opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was a real eye-opener for us. When we first built Glaze, we were thinking like computer scientists. We assumed people would download the app and run it locally, and that most would have a reasonably modern machine, maybe with a decent GPU. Once we started talking to artists, we found that just wasn't the reality for a lot of them.

Many artists are working on older laptops, or on an iPad, or even mostly on their phones. Plenty of them are freelancers or students who are already stretched financially. They're not going to buy a high-end NVIDIA card just to protect their work. On a lot of those machines, running Glaze locally was painfully slow. We're talking long waits per image, sometimes much longer, and for some people it just wouldn't run at all. If you're an artist with a large portfolio, that's a non-starter.

So that pushed us to build WebGlaze. The idea is that artists can submit their artwork through a web interface, and we run the computation on GPUs on our side and send the protected image back to them. It's free, because we felt strongly that the people who most need protection are often the least able to pay for it. We do gate it with an invite system, partly to manage compute costs and partly to make sure it's going to actual human artists rather than being abused.

The broader lesson for me was that you can build the most technically sound tool in the world, but if it doesn't fit the lives of the people you're building it for, it doesn't matter. Accessibility had to be a first-class design goal, not something we tacked on afterward.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains that many artists use older or low-powered devices and cannot afford a high-end GPU, which led the team to offer WebGlaze with computation on their GPUs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that was a real eye-opener for us, honestly. We come from a world where, you know, we have GPU clusters sitting down the hall, and our first instinct was just to think about Glaze as a research artifact—here's the algorithm, here's the code, go run it. And then we started actually talking to artists, and we did surveys with, I think it was over a thousand artists early on, and the picture of what hardware they had was completely different from what we'd assumed.

A huge fraction of them were working on laptops, often older laptops, a lot of them on Macs with no discrete GPU at all. Many of them were on machines that were five, six, seven years old, because an artist's budget goes toward a drawing tablet or a Wacom display or software subscriptions, not toward an NVIDIA card. And a lot of folks were on limited bandwidth, or in parts of the world where they just don't have access to the kind of compute we take for granted in an academic lab.

So that changed a few things. First, we couldn't just assume CUDA. We had to spend a lot of engineering effort making the optimization run on CPU, and later on Apple Silicon, and accept that it might take, you know, tens of minutes per image on an older machine instead of seconds. Which is painful, but it's a tradeoff artists told us they were willing to make.

Second, we had to think really hard about the user experience. These aren't people who want to open a terminal and set up a Python environment. So we built a standalone application with a GUI, a one-click installer, something you download and it just works. That's not glamorous research work, but it was absolutely necessary if we wanted real adoption.

And third, we realized some people simply couldn't run it locally at all, even with all of that. So that's part of what pushed us toward WebGlaze, where we offer it as a free service running on our own hardware, with invitations for artists who verify who they are, so they can upload an image and get it back glazed without needing anything on their end.

The broader lesson for me was that if you're building a tool meant to protect a community, you have to meet that community where they actually are, not where it's convenient for you to imagine they are. Otherwise you've built something that only works for the people who needed it least.

r001.rationale: The response says a huge fraction of artists used older laptops without discrete GPUs because their budgets went to art tools, then explains that artists who still could not run Glaze locally led them to offer WebGlaze on their own hardware.

astra-6.text: We learned that a lot of artists don’t have the kind of computing resources we take for granted as researchers. The computer they use to make art might be an older laptop, without a powerful GPU, and running Glaze locally could be slow or simply impractical. So making the software available to download wasn’t enough. That led us to offer WebGlaze, where we run the computation on our servers and artists can access it through a browser.

r001.rationale: The response says many artists lack powerful GPUs and that local Glaze would be impractical, motivating WebGlaze. It does not say artists could not afford GPU-capable computers.

sol-6.1.text: We initially assumed that artists would have fairly powerful computers, because they’re working with digital images all day. But when we talked to them, we found that a lot were using older laptops, sometimes machines they’d had for many years. They didn’t necessarily have a dedicated GPU or the resources to buy new hardware. So making Glaze available couldn’t just mean putting out software that worked well on our machines. We needed a way for artists to use it without running that computation locally, and that led us to offer WebGlaze, where we do the processing on our servers through a web interface.

r001.rationale: The response says many artists used older laptops, lacked a dedicated GPU or the resources to buy new hardware, and therefore needed server-side processing through WebGlaze.
